before.title: 1.0 Kappa Three-Cylinder Timing Chain and Tensioner Rattle on Cold Start
before.description: The HB20's 1.0-liter Kappa three-cylinder engine (used across both generations, including the 12v aspirated and later TGDI versions) uses a timing chain with a hydraulic tensioner that depends entirely on oil pressure and oil cleanliness. A widely documented complaint among Brazilian owners and independent mechanics is a metallic rattle from the chain side of the engine on cold start, which fades after a few seconds once oil pressure builds. Extended oil-change intervals, wrong viscosity, or low-quality oil clog the tensioner's oil passages, letting the chain slacken and slap against the cover. Left unaddressed, the chain and guides wear prematurely, the noise becomes constant, and in advanced cases timing accuracy is affected. The issue is discussed extensively on Hyundai HB20 Clube forums, the Oficina Brasil professional mechanics forum, and Brazilian automotive sites covering 2012-2024+ cars.
before.solution: If the rattle lasts only a couple of seconds on a cold morning start, it is often hydraulic lifter/tensioner bleed-down and can be managed with strict 5,000-10,000 km oil changes using the correct specification oil. If the noise persists or returns when warm, have the chain, tensioner, and guides inspected. Replacement of the full timing kit (chain, tensioner, guides, gears) with quality parts runs roughly R$2,000-4,000 (parts plus labor) in Brazil. Maintaining clean oil at the correct viscosity is the primary prevention measure since the tensioner is oil-fed.
symptoms: Metallic rattle from the engine for a few seconds on cold start
Chain slap noise from the timing-cover side of the engine
Noise becomes louder or constant as mileage increases
Ticking/rattle worsens when oil changes are overdue
Noise fades once the engine warms and oil pressure stabilizes

before.title: 1.0 TGDI Direct Injection Failure Causing Sudden Loss of Power
before.description: Second-generation HB20s with the 1.0 TGDI turbo direct-injection engine (Smartstream Kappa, introduced for MY2020) show a recurring complaint pattern in Brazil: the injection/check-engine light comes on, the engine loses power or shuts down entirely, and the car must be towed to a dealership — sometimes repeatedly on the same vehicle, including cars with under 30,000 km. Multiple Reclame Aqui complaints describe it as a chronic problem, with owners reporting dealerships keeping large stocks of injection components because of the failure frequency, and Brazilian automotive sites (Grupo Sentinela, Click Petróleo e Gás) list direct-injection failures, power loss, and increased fuel consumption among the most-cited HB20 II defects. Dealers frequently attribute the failures to fuel quality, which has led to warranty disputes; Hyundai has publicly characterized the cases as isolated and covered by the 5-year unlimited-mileage warranty. The direct-injection system (high-pressure pump, injectors) is more complex and more expensive to repair than the older port-injection 1.0.
before.solution: If the injection warning light comes on or the car goes into reduced power, have it scanned and repaired at a Hyundai dealership under the 5-year unlimited-mileage warranty — push back on fuel-quality denials if you fuel at reputable stations, and keep fuel receipts. Repairs typically involve replacing failed injectors, the high-pressure fuel pump, or related sensors and reflashing the ECU. Using good-quality fuel from known stations reduces (but does not eliminate) the risk. Outside warranty, direct-injection component replacement is substantially more expensive than on the aspirated engine, so a pre-purchase scan of injection fault history is advisable on used TGDI cars.
symptoms: Injection/check-engine warning light comes on
Sudden loss of power or limp mode while driving
Engine stalls or shuts down and will not restart
Rough running and increased fuel consumption
Failure recurs after dealership repair

before.title: BlueMedia/BlueNav Infotainment Unit Freezing and Total Failure
before.description: The factory BlueMedia (and BlueNav) multimedia unit fitted to first-generation HB20 trims is the subject of a large, consistent complaint pattern on Reclame Aqui and HB20 owner forums, and Brazilian car-audio specialists have published warnings about buying used Hyundais with the original head unit. Reported failures include the screen freezing, the unit rebooting on its own while driving, switching media sources by itself, sudden volume spikes, losing paired phones and saved settings after restart, CarLink malfunction, and ultimately the unit failing to power on at all. Dealerships acknowledged nationwide defects and issued software updates, but Hyundai later discontinued software support, and the unit (supplied by Motrex) generally cannot be repaired — only replaced. Owners report replacement quotes of roughly R$3,000-6,000, while the multimedia carries a shorter separate warranty (24 months / 40,000 km) than the car's 5-year warranty, which is the core of many complaints describing it as a hidden defect.
before.solution: First try the dealership software update if one is still available for the unit's version, and check for blown fuses if the unit is completely dead. If the unit has failed outside its 24-month accessory warranty, the practical fix most Brazilian owners choose is replacing the factory head unit with a quality aftermarket Android unit with a model-specific fascia kit (typically R$1,500-3,000 installed), since the original Motrex unit is unrepairable, replacement units cost R$3,000-6,000, and factory software support has been discontinued. Document the failure and complaint history if pursuing a hidden-defect (vício oculto) claim.
symptoms: Touchscreen freezes and stops responding
Unit reboots by itself while driving
Media source changes or volume spikes on its own
Bluetooth pairings and settings lost after restart
Unit no longer powers on at all

before.title: Clutch Judder and Vibration When Pulling Away (1.0 Manual)
before.description: Shuddering or juddering when launching from a stop is one of the most repeated complaints from first-generation HB20 owners with the 1.0 manual powertrain, documented in Revista Carro's technical Q&A column, HB20 Clube forum threads, and a recurring pattern of Reclame Aqui complaints describing it as a chronic defect. The technical consensus reported by Revista Carro is that in roughly 90% of cases the cause is a warped or contaminated clutch disc; a damaged flywheel surface can also cause the irregular engagement. Some owners report the judder returning even after a clutch kit replacement, and others report the pedal becoming stiff over time. Because Hyundai treats the clutch as a wear item with only 90 days of warranty coverage, many owners ended up paying for the repair themselves, fueling the complaint volume.
before.solution: Replace the clutch kit (disc, pressure plate, release bearing) and inspect the flywheel surface for heat spots, warping, or scoring — resurface or replace it if damaged, otherwise the judder will return with the new clutch. Insist on a road test with a dealership technician if the car is still inside the 5-year vehicle warranty window, as judder on takeoff is not normal behavior. A quality clutch kit plus labor typically runs about R$1,800-3,500 in Brazil; more if the flywheel must be replaced.
symptoms: Car shudders or judders when pulling away in first gear
Vibration on takeoff that worsens on uphill starts
Clutch pedal becomes stiff or sticks down over time
Judder returns shortly after a clutch replacement
Vibration felt through the floor and shift lever during engagement

before.title: Recall: Automatic Transmission Electric Oil Pump Control Module Short Circuit (Fire Risk)
before.description: Hyundai Motor Brasil recalled 2023-2024 HB20 and HB20S vehicles manufactured from December 20, 2022 through September 27, 2023. Hyundai says a nonconformity in the automatic transmission electric oil-pump control module can cause an internal short circuit. In an extreme case, that can cause a fire and property damage or serious or fatal injury to occupants or other people.
before.solution: Schedule the free recall inspection with a Hyundai Motor Brasil dealer. Hyundai says the dealer will inspect the vehicle and replace the automatic-transmission electric oil-pump control module if necessary; the service takes about two hours. The notice identifies the non-sequential last-eight-digit chassis range PP395536 through RP509630 for HB20 and HB20S.

before.title: Recall: Brake Booster Vacuum Control Valve Can Dry Out and Harden the Brake Pedal (1.0 Turbo)
before.description: Hyundai Motor Brasil recalled 2016-2018 HB20 and HB20S vehicles with the 1.0 Turbo engine and six-speed manual transmission, manufactured from January 28, 2016 through February 5, 2018. Hyundai says heat exposure near the catalytic converter can dry the brake-booster vacuum control valve. A whistle and unstable idle can precede reduced brake-booster vacuum, a harder brake pedal, greater required pedal force and increased stopping time and distance. The brakes continue to operate, but the condition increases crash risk.
before.solution: Hyundai advises stopping use and contacting a dealer immediately if a whistle from the engine area and unstable idle occur. The free recall service inspects the brake-booster vacuum control valve. If the valve is undamaged, the dealer adds a thermal insulator; if it is damaged, the dealer replaces it and adds the insulator. Hyundai estimates about 30 minutes for the service.
symptoms: Whistling noise from the engine area
Unstable or oscillating idle
Harder brake pedal
More pedal force required to stop
Increased stopping time and distance
